y-m-05-01.title: Does having 3 vertices make a shape a triangle?
y-m-05-01.goal: Think about what conditions a shape needs to be a triangle. Each time you meet a new shape, check whether anything is missing from Arin's statement, and fix your judgment.
y-m-05-01.material: Arin said, "A shape with 3 vertices is a triangle." There are no pictures, so the shapes are described in words. A side is a line that goes around a shape, and a vertex is a pointed spot where two sides meet.
y-m-05-01.thinking.0: Finding the missing condition in a friend's statement
y-m-05-01.thinking.1: Looking at a new shape and fixing your judgment
y-m-05-01.thinking.2: Sorting out which conditions are needed and which are not
y-m-05-01.prereq.0: Knowing what sides (lines that go around a shape) and vertices (points where two sides meet) are (Grade 2 level)
y-m-05-01.s.s1.prompt: Each time another shape description is added, sort out your thinking about Arin's statement.
y-m-05-01.s.s1.hint.0: Check, one by one, whether the shapes you have seen so far disagree with Arin's statement.
y-m-05-01.s.s1.hint.1: In the new description, look at what the sides are like and whether the ends of the sides are all connected.
y-m-05-01.s.s1.st.0.info: Figure 가 is made of 3 straight lines connected with no gaps, going all the way around. It also has 3 vertices.
y-m-05-01.s.s1.st.0.after: Arin's statement is right for Figure 가. But being right for one shape does not mean it is right for every shape.
y-m-05-01.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It can be trusted. Figure 가 is a triangle with 3 vertices.
y-m-05-01.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This thinking sees that the statement is right in one example. Testing other shapes would make it more certain.
y-m-05-01.s.s1.st.0.o.b: We do not know yet. We need to look at more shapes.
y-m-05-01.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This thinking sees that one example is hard to use to say something about "all shapes."
y-m-05-01.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It is wrong. You cannot recognize a triangle by its vertices.
y-m-05-01.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This thinking decides the statement is wrong first, without looking at the shapes.
y-m-05-01.s.s1.st.1.info: Figure 나 has 3 pointed vertices. But one of its three sides curves outward in a round shape.
y-m-05-01.s.s1.st.1.ask: What happens to Arin's statement now?
y-m-05-01.s.s1.st.1.after: Figure 나 has 3 vertices but is not a triangle. Arin's statement is missing the condition "the sides are straight lines."
y-m-05-01.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The vertices should be counted as 4, not 3.
y-m-05-01.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This thinking changes the number to fit the statement, even though the description says there are 3 vertices.
y-m-05-01.s.s1.st.1.o.b: It is still right. It has 3 vertices, so it is a triangle.
y-m-05-01.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This thinking looks only at the number of vertices and not at the shape of the sides.
y-m-05-01.s.s1.st.1.o.c: A shape can have 3 vertices and still not be a triangle.
y-m-05-01.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This thinking sees that you must look at the shape of the sides, not only the number of vertices.
y-m-05-01.s.s1.st.2.info: Figure 다 is made of 3 straight lines, but it is broken in one place, so it does not go all the way around.
y-m-05-01.s.s1.st.2.after: If it is broken even in one place, it is not a shape that goes all the way around. Even with 3 straight lines, it is not a triangle.
y-m-05-01.s.s1.st.2.o.a: It is not a triangle. It does not enclose without gaps.
y-m-05-01.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This thinking also looks at the condition that even with 3 straight lines, they must enclose the shape.
y-m-05-01.s.s1.st.2.o.b: It is a triangle. It is a shape made of 3 straight lines.
y-m-05-01.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This thinking looks only at the number and shape of the lines, not at whether they are connected.
y-m-05-01.s.s1.st.2.o.c: If the broken gap is very small, it is a triangle.
y-m-05-01.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This thinking treats a small gap as the same as enclosing. Think about whether a shape that is broken can be called closed.
y-m-05-01.s.s1.reflect: At first, having 3 vertices seemed like enough. But when we met a shape with a round side and a shape that was broken, we learned that a condition was missing. To find out whether a statement is right, we should look not only for examples that fit but also for examples that do not.
y-m-05-01.s.s2.prompt: Choose everything that a shape must have in order to be a triangle.
y-m-05-01.s.s2.hint.0: Think again about Figures 가, 나, and 다, and compare when a shape was a triangle and when it was not.
y-m-05-01.s.s2.hint.1: For the shapes that are not triangles, pick out one by one what was missing.
y-m-05-01.s.s2.o.a: All three sides have the same length.
y-m-05-01.s.s2.r.a: This thinking pictured only triangles with equal sides. Think about whether there are triangles whose sides have different lengths.
y-m-05-01.s.s2.r.b: This thinking looked at the shape of the sides as a condition.
y-m-05-01.s.s2.o.c: It is enclosed all the way around with no gaps.
y-m-05-01.s.s2.r.c: This thinking looked at being closed as a condition.
y-m-05-01.s.s2.o.d: One corner is a square corner.
y-m-05-01.s.s2.r.d: This thinking pictured only triangles with a square corner. Also picture a triangle whose corners are only pointed.
y-m-05-01.s.s2.r.e: This thinking looked at the number of sides as a condition.
y-m-05-01.s.s2.explain: A triangle is a shape enclosed all the way around, with no gaps, by 3 straight lines. All sides being the same length or having a square corner is not a required condition for a triangle.
y-m-05-01.s.s2.acc.0: The two conditions about being enclosed by straight lines are right. The condition that there are 3 sides must also be there for it to be a triangle.

y-m-05-02.title: How many ways are there to use up all the sticks?
y-m-05-02.topic: Number of sides of triangles and quadrilaterals
y-m-05-02.goal: Using the number of sticks needed for a triangle and a quadrilateral, find different ways to use up all 31 sticks, and describe the rule for changing from one way to another.
y-m-05-02.material: There are 31 sticks of the same length. You can make one triangle with 3 sticks and one quadrilateral with 4 sticks. The sticks used for one shape are used only for that shape (no sticks are shared with other shapes). You want to use all 31 sticks with none left over, and make at least 1 triangle and at least 1 quadrilateral.
y-m-05-02.thinking.0: Finding how many sticks each shape needs
y-m-05-02.thinking.1: Making several ways that fit the conditions
y-m-05-02.thinking.2: Finding a rule for changing one way into another
y-m-05-02.prereq.0: Knowing that a triangle has 3 sides and a quadrilateral has 4 sides (Grade 2 level)
y-m-05-02.prereq.1: Adding two-digit numbers, and adding the same number many times
y-m-05-02.s.s1.prompt: Gaon made 6 triangles and 3 quadrilaterals. Did Gaon use up all 31 sticks?
y-m-05-02.s.s1.hint.0: First count how many sticks in all are needed for 6 triangles.
y-m-05-02.s.s1.hint.1: Also count the sticks needed for 3 quadrilaterals, then add the two numbers and compare with 31.
y-m-05-02.s.s1.explain: 6 triangles need 18 sticks and 3 quadrilaterals need 12 sticks, so 30 sticks are used in all. If 30 of the 31 sticks are used, 1 is left over.
y-m-05-02.s.s2.prompt: Make t triangles and s quadrilaterals, and find three different ways to use up all 31 sticks. (t and s are each natural numbers that are at least 1.)
y-m-05-02.s.s2.hint.0: Decide the number of triangles first, then find how many sticks are left for the quadrilaterals.
y-m-05-02.s.s2.hint.1: Check how many quadrilaterals you can make with the leftover sticks, and whether no sticks are left over.
y-m-05-02.s.s2.ok.c1: There is at least 1 triangle and at least 1 quadrilateral.
y-m-05-02.s.s2.fail.c1: The numbers of triangles and quadrilaterals must each be a natural number that is at least 1.
y-m-05-02.s.s2.ok.c2: Use all 31 sticks with none left over.
y-m-05-02.s.s2.fail.c2: Sticks are left over or run short. Add the sticks needed for the triangles and the sticks needed for the quadrilaterals, and check whether the total is 31.
y-m-05-02.s.s2.explain: These are possible: 9 triangles and 1 quadrilateral (27+4), 5 triangles and 4 quadrilaterals (15+16), 1 triangle and 7 quadrilaterals (3+28). If there is at least 1 of each, these three are the only ways.
y-m-05-02.s.s2.because.prompt: After finding one way, explain how to quickly find another way while still using exactly 31 sticks.
y-m-05-02.s.s2.because.hint.0: Count how many sticks are left over if you take away some of the triangles from the way you found.
y-m-05-02.s.s2.because.hint.1: Check how many more quadrilaterals you can make with those sticks.
y-m-05-02.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: If you take away ... triangles, ...
y-m-05-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you check again that the new way also uses 31 sticks?
y-m-05-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you say how the numbers of triangles and quadrilaterals swap with each other?
y-m-05-02.s.s2.because.model.0: If you take away 4 triangles, 12 sticks are left. You can make 3 quadrilaterals with those sticks, so you can change 4 triangles into 3 quadrilaterals.
y-m-05-02.s.s2.because.model.1: Take away triangles one at a time and count how many quadrilaterals you gain from the sticks. 4 triangles and 3 quadrilaterals both use 12 sticks, so swapping them keeps the total at 31.
y-m-05-02.s.s1.r.a: This is thinking that found the number of sticks for each shape, added them, and compared with 31.
y-m-05-02.s.s1.o.b: All the sticks were used up with none left
y-m-05-02.s.s1.r.b: This is thinking that looked only at the number of shapes, such as there being 9 shapes made in all, or judged without checking the number of sticks.
y-m-05-02.s.s1.r.c: This is thinking that miscounted the number of sticks needed for a triangle or a quadrilateral once. Count again for each shape.
y-m-05-02.s.s2.because.model.2: If you remove 4 triangles (12 sticks) and use those sticks to make 3 quadrilaterals, you use all 31 as they are.

y-m-05-03.title: How many building blocks are there if we only see the front?
y-m-05-03.topic: A shape made of building blocks
y-m-05-03.goal: Realize that the total number of building blocks cannot be decided from the front view alone, and find for yourself the information that lets you decide it and the numbers that are possible.
y-m-05-03.material: Building blocks are wooden cubes of the same size. There are 3 spots side by side from left to right. In the front row, the left spot has 2 blocks (2 levels), the middle spot has 1, and the right spot has 1, so the front row has 4 blocks in all. From the front, it looks like stairs, with the left side one level higher. There may be a back row behind the front row, but it is hidden by the front row and cannot be seen. If there is a back row, each spot is stacked no higher than the same spot in the front row (if it were higher, you could see it from the front). Blocks do not float in the air, and there are only two rows, a front row and a back row.
y-m-05-03.thinking.0: Telling apart what you can see and what is hidden
y-m-05-03.thinking.1: Choosing the information needed to decide the number
y-m-05-03.prereq.0: Having made shapes with building blocks (Grade 2 level)
y-m-05-03.s.s1.prompt: Jihu said, "There are 4 building blocks in all." With only what we know now, can we say this for sure?
y-m-05-03.s.s1.hint.0: Separate the building blocks you can see from the hidden places you cannot see.
y-m-05-03.s.s1.hint.1: Picture the case where the back row has no blocks at all and the case where it has some.
y-m-05-03.s.s1.o.a: There are exactly 4. What you can see is everything.
y-m-05-03.s.s1.r.a: This thinking assumes what you can see is everything. Think about what might be in the hidden places.
y-m-05-03.s.s1.o.b: There are at least 4. We do not know if there is a back row.
y-m-05-03.s.s1.r.b: This thinking judges by separating the part you can see from the hidden part.
y-m-05-03.s.s1.o.c: There must be blocks in the back row, so there are at least 5.
y-m-05-03.s.s1.r.c: This thinking assumes there must be blocks in the hidden place. Think about whether the back row could be empty.
y-m-05-03.s.s1.explain: The 4 blocks in the front row are certain, but we cannot see whether there is a back row. So we can only say there are at least 4.
y-m-05-03.s.s2.prompt: Choose all the pieces of information such that being told just one more of them lets you decide the total number of building blocks.
y-m-05-03.s.s2.hint.0: See whether that information lets you know the number of blocks in the back row.
y-m-05-03.s.s2.hint.1: Sort out whether it only shows something you already know, or has nothing to do with the number.
y-m-05-03.s.s2.r.a: This thinking chose information that has nothing to do with the number. Think about whether color tells you the hidden number.
y-m-05-03.s.s2.o.b: How many levels each spot in the back row has
y-m-05-03.s.s2.r.b: This thinking sees that the height of each spot in the back row lets you find the number in the back row.
y-m-05-03.s.s2.r.c: This thinking missed that the side view shows only the tallest level of each row. Think about whether it decides how many are in the back row.
y-m-05-03.s.s2.o.d: The number of blocks in the back row
y-m-05-03.s.s2.r.d: This thinking sees that if you know the number in the back row, you can add it to the front row to find the total.
y-m-05-03.s.s2.o.e: Showing the front view one more time
y-m-05-03.s.s2.r.e: This thinking missed that looking again at information you already know is not new information.
y-m-05-03.s.s2.explain: The front row is already known to have 4. If you know the number in the back row or the number of levels at each spot, the total is decided. Color, the side view, or looking at the front view again cannot by themselves decide the number in the back row.
y-m-05-03.s.s2.acc.0: If you know the number of levels at each spot in the back row, you can decide the number. Being told the number in the back row directly does the same job.
y-m-05-03.s.s2.acc.1: If you know the number in the back row, you can decide it. Being told the number of levels at each spot does the same job.
y-m-05-03.s.s3.prompt: Find three cases where the front view is the same as at first but the total number n of building blocks is different. (There is at most one back row, and each spot in the back row is no higher than the same spot in the front row. There does not have to be a back row.)
y-m-05-03.s.s3.hint.0: Think about the case where you put the fewest blocks in the back row and the case where you put the most.
y-m-05-03.s.s3.hint.1: Work out the highest level each of the three spots in the back row can have.
y-m-05-03.s.s3.ok.c1: The number is a natural number.
y-m-05-03.s.s3.fail.c1: The number of building blocks must be a natural number.
y-m-05-03.s.s3.ok.c2: It is not less than the 4 in the front row.
y-m-05-03.s.s3.fail.c2: The front row already has 4, so the total cannot be less than 4.
y-m-05-03.s.s3.ok.c3: The back row does not go beyond the front row.
y-m-05-03.s.s3.fail.c3: Each spot in the back row cannot be higher than the same spot in the front row, so this number cannot be made.
y-m-05-03.s.s3.explain: With no back row, there are 4. If the back row has the same shape as the front row (2, 1, 1), there are 4 more, making 8. Any number from 4 to 8 can be made.
y-m-05-03.s.s3.because.prompt: Write how many blocks there are in the case where you stack the most, and explain why you cannot stack more than that.
y-m-05-03.s.s3.because.hint.0: Count how many there are if you stack the left, middle, and right spots of the back row to the same height as the front row.
y-m-05-03.s.s3.because.hint.1: Picture how the view from the front would change if you stacked one spot of the back row higher than the front row.
y-m-05-03.s.s3.because.placeholder: Example: The most is ... blocks. This is because ...
y-m-05-03.s.s3.because.selfAssess.0: Did you think about the case where all three spots in the back row are stacked as high as the front row?
y-m-05-03.s.s3.because.selfAssess.1: Did you say that stacking higher would change the view from the front?
y-m-05-03.s.s3.because.model.0: If you stack the back row like the front row, with 2 on the left, 1 in the middle, and 1 on the right, you get 4 more, so there are 8 in all. If you make the back row higher, the view from the front changes.
y-m-05-03.s.s3.because.model.1: The front row has 4 and the back row can only be stacked as high as the front row, so the most is 8. If you stack higher than that, it can be seen from the front too.

y-m-05-04.goal: Realize that even if a shape looks like a square, you must count its sides and vertices to name it. Find the wrong solution and rewrite it as a note.
y-m-05-04.thinking.0: Finding the first wrong line in the solution
y-m-05-04.thinking.1: Naming a shape by its number of sides, not its looks
y-m-05-04.thinking.2: Fixing a wrong solution and passing it on
y-m-05-04.prereq.0: Having heard the names triangle, quadrilateral, pentagon, and hexagon (Grade 2 level)
y-m-05-04.prereq.1: Knowing what sides and vertices are
y-m-05-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first line in Hangyeol's solution where the reasoning goes wrong. (Count the lines starting from number 1.)
y-m-05-04.s.s1.hint.0: Tell apart whether each line is a fact from counting Figure 가 or an idea from its looks.
y-m-05-04.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether the number counted in an earlier line fits what a later line says.
y-m-05-04.s.s1.line.0: I counted the sides of Figure 가 and there are 6, and there are also 6 vertices.
y-m-05-04.s.s1.line.1: Figure 가 is shaped like a big square with a corner taken out.
y-m-05-04.s.s1.line.2: It came from a square shape, so Figure 가 is a quadrilateral.
y-m-05-04.s.s1.line.3: So Figure 가 is a shape with 4 sides.
y-m-05-04.s.s2.prompt: Choose the right name for Figure 가 and the right reason for calling it that.
y-m-05-04.s.s2.hint.0: Check again in line 1 how many sides Figure 가 has in all.
y-m-05-04.s.s2.hint.1: Compare the number of sides each choice mentions with Figure 가.
y-m-05-04.s.s2.o.c: Pentagon: If you leave out the corner that was taken out, there are 5.
y-m-05-04.s.s2.r.c: This thinking estimated the number of sides by subtracting or adding the place that was taken out. Count the actual lines one by one.
y-m-05-04.s.s2.explain: Figure 가 has 6 sides and 6 vertices, so it is a hexagon.
y-m-05-04.s.s3.prompt: Write a note to Hangyeol. Tell him what to check to know whether a shape is a quadrilateral.
y-m-05-04.s.s3.hint.0: Compare, using Figure 가, whether looking like a square is the same as being a quadrilateral.
y-m-05-04.s.s3.hint.1: In the note, write both what to check and how many there should be.
y-m-05-04.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Hangyeol, to know if it is a quadrilateral, ...
y-m-05-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you base your note on the numbers counted, not on the looks?
y-m-05-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you use the numbers of Figure 가 to say why Figure 가 is not a quadrilateral?
y-m-05-04.s.s3.model.0: Hangyeol, even if it looks like a square, you cannot say it is a quadrilateral. You have to count whether it has 4 sides and 4 vertices. Figure 가 has 6, so it is not a quadrilateral.
y-m-05-04.s.s3.model.1: To know if it is a quadrilateral, count whether there are four straight lines (sides). Figure 가 has six, so it is not a quadrilateral but a hexagon.
y-m-05-04.title: What Is the Name of Shape 가?
y-m-05-04.material: Shape 가 is shaped like the letter 'ㄴ'. It is a big square with a small square taken away from one corner. Hangyeol solved as below to decide the name of shape 가.
y-m-05-04.s.s1.explain: It first goes wrong in line 3. In line 1 the sides were counted as 6, so it cannot be a quadrilateral, which has 4 sides. What decides the name is not where it came from but how many sides and vertices it has now. Line 4 is a conclusion that contradicts the number counted in line 1, so it is a mistake that follows after line 3.
y-m-05-04.s.s2.o.a: Quadrilateral: it was taken away from a square
y-m-05-04.s.s2.r.a: This is thinking that if the way it was made is the same, the name is the same. Count how many sides there are now.
y-m-05-04.s.s2.o.b: Hexagon: it has 6 sides and 6 vertices
y-m-05-04.s.s2.r.b: This is thinking that decided the name by counting the number of sides and vertices.

y-m-05-05.title: Will cutting once always make a triangle?
y-m-05-05.topic: Pieces made by cutting a square
y-m-05-05.goal: Show with one counterexample that the statement "If you cut a square once in a straight line, a triangle is sure to appear" is wrong, and fix the statement so it is right.
y-m-05-05.material: There is a square piece of colored paper with sides of 6cm. You connect point P on the top side and point Q on the bottom side with a straight line and cut. Point P is x cm to the right of the left end of the top side, and point Q is y cm to the right of the left end of the bottom side. x and y are natural numbers from 0cm to 6cm, and if it is 0cm or 6cm, the point is at the end of the edge (a vertex). Seoyun said, "If you cut a square once in a straight line, one of the pieces is sure to be a triangle."
y-m-05-05.thinking.0: Sorting out what is needed to show the statement is wrong
y-m-05-05.thinking.1: Making a counterexample that follows the conditions
y-m-05-05.thinking.2: Fixing the statement so it is right
y-m-05-05.prereq.0: Knowing the number of sides of triangles and quadrilaterals (Grade 2 level)
y-m-05-05.prereq.1: Reading the marks on a ruler and telling length in cm
y-m-05-05.s.s1.prompt: What do you have to show to say Seoyun's statement is wrong?
y-m-05-05.s.s1.hint.0: Think about what kind of cut must exist, even just one, for "is sure to have" to be broken.
y-m-05-05.s.s1.hint.1: Think about what happens to the word "sure" if you show many cuts that make a triangle.
y-m-05-05.s.s1.o.a: Show many different cuts that make a triangle.
y-m-05-05.s.s1.r.a: This thinking assumes that collecting many examples that fit shows the statement is wrong. Examples that fit support the statement.
y-m-05-05.s.s1.o.b: Try every possible cut, without missing any.
y-m-05-05.s.s1.r.b: This thinking tries every case, but even one example that does not fit is enough.
y-m-05-05.s.s1.o.c: Show one cut that does not make a triangle.
y-m-05-05.s.s1.r.c: This thinking sees that the word "sure" is broken by a single example that does not fit.
y-m-05-05.s.s1.explain: The statement "is sure to have" is wrong if there is even just one cut that makes no triangle at all. No matter how many examples that fit you collect, you cannot show that the statement is always right.
y-m-05-05.s.s2.prompt: Find three different ways to cut so that both pieces are quadrilaterals. Just decide x for point P and y for point Q. (x and y are natural numbers from 0 to 6.)
y-m-05-05.s.s2.hint.0: Look at what shape the pieces become when point P or point Q is at the end of an edge.
y-m-05-05.s.s2.hint.1: When points P and Q are not at the end of an edge, count how many sides each piece has.
y-m-05-05.s.s2.var.x: Position x (cm) of point P on the top side
y-m-05-05.s.s2.var.y: Position y (cm) of point Q on the bottom side
y-m-05-05.s.s2.ok.c1: x and y are natural numbers from 0 to 6.
y-m-05-05.s.s2.fail.c1: x and y must be natural numbers from 0 to 6.
y-m-05-05.s.s2.ok.c2: Neither point is at the end of an edge, so both pieces are quadrilaterals.
y-m-05-05.s.s2.fail.c2: Because a point is at the end of an edge, a triangle piece appears, or it is the same as not cutting. Try moving points P and Q to places that are not the end of an edge.
y-m-05-05.s.s2.explain: If points P and Q are both not at the end of an edge, both pieces are quadrilaterals. For example, (3, 3) is the case of cutting straight through the middle. If a point is at the end of an edge (for example, 0 and 6), a triangle piece appears.
y-m-05-05.s.s2.because.prompt: Pick one of the cuts you found above and write why you can say Seoyun's statement is wrong.
y-m-05-05.s.s2.because.hint.0: First say the names of the two pieces in the cut you picked.
y-m-05-05.s.s2.because.hint.1: Think about what "sure" means in Seoyun's statement and compare it with the cut you picked.
y-m-05-05.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: If you cut with P at ...cm and Q at ...cm, ...
y-m-05-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you say x and y (or the positions) of the cut you picked?
y-m-05-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you say that even one example is enough to show that "is sure to have" is wrong?
y-m-05-05.s.s2.because.model.0: If you cut by connecting P and Q both at the 3cm spot, both pieces are quadrilaterals, so there is no triangle at all. So the statement "is sure to have" is wrong.
y-m-05-05.s.s2.because.model.1: If you connect the 2cm point on the top side and the 4cm point on the bottom side, both pieces are quadrilaterals with 4 sides. No triangle appears, so Seoyun's statement is wrong.
y-m-05-05.s.s3.prompt: We want to fix Seoyun's statement so it is right. Choose the statement that is right.
y-m-05-05.s.s3.hint.0: Put side by side the cuts you have found so far that made a triangle and those that did not.
y-m-05-05.s.s3.hint.1: Test one by one whether each sentence fits both cases.
y-m-05-05.s.s3.o.a: If you cut once in a straight line, a triangle may appear.
y-m-05-05.s.s3.r.a: This thinking fixed the statement by including both the cases where a triangle appears and where it does not.
y-m-05-05.s.s3.o.b: If you cut once in a straight line, the pieces are always quadrilaterals.
y-m-05-05.s.s3.r.b: This thinking saw only examples with quadrilaterals and assumed every cut is like that. What happens if you cut at the edges?
y-m-05-05.s.s3.o.c: If you cut once in a straight line, a triangle never appears.
y-m-05-05.s.s3.r.c: This thinking saw only examples with no triangle and assumed every cut is like that. What happens if you connect one edge to another?
y-m-05-05.s.s3.explain: If you connect opposite edges, a triangle appears, and if you connect places that are not edges, a quadrilateral appears. So "a triangle may appear" is the right statement.

y-m-05-06.title: The desk measured in hand spans: which is longer?
y-m-05-06.goal: Realize that lengths measured by different people with their own hand spans cannot be compared by the number of spans alone. Fix your judgment as information is added, and make cases where the lengths are the same.
y-m-05-06.material: Gaeun and Narae each measured the long side of a desk with their own hand span (the length from thumb to little finger spread wide). One person's span stays nearly the same length each time. A centimeter (cm) is a unit that shows length.
y-m-05-06.thinking.0: Telling apart measuring with the same standard and with a different standard
y-m-05-06.thinking.1: Adjusting how sure you are as new information comes in
y-m-05-06.thinking.2: Making cases where the lengths are the same
y-m-05-06.prereq.0: Having measured length with hand spans or the body
y-m-05-06.prereq.1: Knowing cm as a unit of length
y-m-05-06.prereq.2: Adding the same number many times (Grade 2 level)
y-m-05-06.s.s1.prompt: Each time one piece of information is added, sort out your thinking about which desk is longer.
y-m-05-06.s.s1.hint.0: First check who measured and whether the length of one hand span is the same standard.
y-m-05-06.s.s1.hint.1: With the new information, see whether the lengths of the two desks can be shown in the same unit (cm).
y-m-05-06.s.s1.st.0.info: Desk 가 is 4 spans and Desk 나 is 3 spans. Gaeun measured both desks with her own hand span.
y-m-05-06.s.s1.st.0.after: The same person measured with the same span, so 4 spans is longer than 3 spans.
y-m-05-06.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This thinking sees that since the same person measured with the same span, the one with more spans is longer.
y-m-05-06.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This thinking assumes the one with fewer spans is longer. Think again about the case measured with the same span.
y-m-05-06.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This thinking did not use the information that the same person measured with the same span.
y-m-05-06.s.s1.st.1.info: It turns out that Gaeun measured Desk 가 and Narae measured Desk 나, each with her own hand span. We do not yet know how long their spans are.
y-m-05-06.s.s1.st.1.after: If different people measured with their own spans, you cannot say for sure from the number of spans alone. The first judgment might be right, but you need to know the span lengths to check.
y-m-05-06.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Desk 가 seems longer, but we are not sure.
y-m-05-06.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This thinking keeps the first judgment but lowers how sure it is.
y-m-05-06.s.s1.st.1.o.b: We cannot tell. We do not know the length of the two people's spans.
y-m-05-06.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This thinking sees that values measured with different standards cannot be compared.
y-m-05-06.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This thinking flipped the first judgment after seeing the new information, but it is hard to give a reason for it.
y-m-05-06.s.s1.st.2.info: Gaeun's hand span is 9cm, and Narae's hand span is 13cm.
y-m-05-06.s.s1.st.2.ask: What happens if you show the lengths of the two desks in cm and compare them?
y-m-05-06.s.s1.st.2.after: Desk 가 is 9+9+9+9=36cm and Desk 나 is 13+13+13=39cm. Even with fewer spans, if each span is longer, that desk can be the longer one.
y-m-05-06.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This thinking estimated that the difference in span length matches the difference in the number of spans.
y-m-05-06.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This thinking assumes the one with more spans is still the longer one.
y-m-05-06.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This thinking found the length of each desk in cm and compared them.
y-m-05-06.s.s1.reflect: When the same person measured, we could compare by the number of spans. But when different people measured with their own spans, it was hard to say for sure. We could compare only after we knew the length of one span in the same unit (cm).
y-m-05-06.s.s2.prompt: If Desk 가 (4 spans) and Desk 나 (3 spans) have the same length, find three different pairs of values for Gaeun's hand span a cm and Narae's hand span b cm. (Both people's hand spans are natural numbers from 8cm to 20cm.)
y-m-05-06.s.s2.hint.0: Decide a, find how many cm Gaeun's 4 spans are, then find the b that makes Narae's 3 spans that same length.
y-m-05-06.s.s2.hint.1: Check that b is a natural number and at most 20.
y-m-05-06.s.s2.ok.c1: Both people's hand spans are natural numbers from 8cm to 20cm.
y-m-05-06.s.s2.fail.c1: A hand span must be a natural number from 8cm to 20cm.
y-m-05-06.s.s2.ok.c2: 4 spans and 3 spans are the same length.
y-m-05-06.s.s2.fail.c2: The lengths of the two desks are not the same. Find how many cm Gaeun's 4 spans and Narae's 3 spans are, and compare them.
y-m-05-06.s.s2.explain: If Gaeun's span is 9cm and Narae's is 12cm, both are 36cm, the same. 12cm and 16cm (48cm), and 15cm and 20cm (60cm) are also possible. Between 8cm and 20cm, these three are the only ones.
y-m-05-06.s.s2.because.prompt: Write why two desks can have the same length even though the numbers of spans are different, 4 and 3.
y-m-05-06.s.s2.because.hint.0: Pick one pair you found above and put Gaeun's span and Narae's span side by side.
y-m-05-06.s.s2.because.hint.1: Compare what the span is like for the one who measured fewer times.
y-m-05-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you say that one person's hand span is longer?
y-m-05-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you say that the one who measured fewer times must have the longer span for the lengths to be the same?
y-m-05-06.s.s2.because.model.0: Narae's hand span is longer than Gaeun's, so even measuring only 3 times can give the same length as Gaeun measuring 4 times.
y-m-05-06.s.s2.because.model.1: If Gaeun's span is 9cm and Narae's span is 12cm, adding 9 four times and 12 three times both give 36cm, the same. If the span is bigger, fewer measurements can give the same length.
y-m-05-06.s.s2.because.model.2: The lengths of spans differ from person to person, so if Narae's span is longer, the same length takes fewer spans.

y-m-05-07.title: How can we count the triangles in a square without missing any?
y-m-05-07.goal: Compare ways of counting the big and small triangles in a picture without missing any or counting any twice, fix a wrong count, and make your own counting method for a different picture.
y-m-05-07.material: Starting from the top left and going clockwise, call the four vertices of a square piece of paper ㄱ, ㄴ, ㄷ, and ㄹ. Join ㄱ to ㄷ and ㄴ to ㄹ with straight lines, and the two lines meet at the center point ㅁ. We want to count all the big and small triangles that can be found in this picture. All three sides of a triangle must lie on lines drawn in the picture. (ㄱ is read giyeok, ㄴ is read nieun, ㄷ is read digeut, ㄹ is read rieul, and ㅁ is read mieum.)
y-m-05-07.thinking.1: Finding the wrong line in a count
y-m-05-07.thinking.2: Applying a counting method to a new picture
y-m-05-07.prereq.0: Knowing that a triangle is a shape enclosed by 3 straight lines (Grade 2 level)
y-m-05-07.s.s1.prompt: Four friends described how they count triangles. Choose all the methods that can count every triangle without missing any or counting any twice.
y-m-05-07.s.s1.hint.0: For each method, picture which triangles might be missed.
y-m-05-07.s.s1.hint.1: See whether the triangles counted by each method can be told apart without overlapping.
y-m-05-07.s.s1.o.a: Seojin: Count only the smallest triangles.
y-m-05-07.s.s1.r.a: This thinking does not count the big triangles made by joining two small triangles.
y-m-05-07.s.s1.o.b: Daon: Count the small ones first, then count the ones made of two small ones joined.
y-m-05-07.s.s1.r.b: This thinking sorted by size and counted in order.
y-m-05-07.s.s1.o.c: Hajun: Pick 3 of the 5 points at a time, but leave out three points on one straight line.
y-m-05-07.s.s1.r.c: This thinking counts without missing any by picking points, and sorts out the cases that do not make a triangle.
y-m-05-07.s.s1.o.d: Yuna: Count whatever catches the eye.
y-m-05-07.s.s1.r.d: This thinking has no order or rule, so it may miss some or count some twice.
y-m-05-07.s.s1.explain: Counting in order by size, and picking 3 points at a time while leaving out three points on one straight line, can both count every triangle. Counting only the smallest ones, or counting whatever catches the eye, can miss some.
y-m-05-07.s.s1.acc.0: Daon's method can count them all. Hajun's method can count them all too.
y-m-05-07.s.s1.acc.1: Hajun's method can count them all. Daon's method can count them all too.
y-m-05-07.s.s2.prompt: Minu picked 3 of the 5 points at a time and counted triangles. Choose the first line that is wrong. (Count the lines starting from number 1.)
y-m-05-07.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether the numbers in the addition on the last line match the earlier lines.
y-m-05-07.s.s2.line.0: The small triangles are ㄱㄴㅁ, ㄴㄷㅁ, ㄷㄹㅁ, and ㄹㄱㅁ, so there are 4.
y-m-05-07.s.s2.line.1: The big triangles made of two small triangles joined are ㄱㄴㄷ, ㄴㄷㄹ, ㄷㄹㄱ, and ㄹㄱㄴ, so there are 4.
y-m-05-07.s.s2.line.2: ㄱㅁㄷ is also 3 points picked, so it is a triangle.
y-m-05-07.s.s2.line.3: So there are 4+4+1=9 triangles in all.
y-m-05-07.s.s3.prompt: This time, in the square only ㄱ and ㄷ are joined by a straight line, and ㄴ and ㄹ are not joined. Write how many triangles there are in all, and write the way you counted without missing any.
y-m-05-07.s.s3.hint.0: Write down every way to pick 3 of the 4 points, and check one by one whether all three sides of the three points you picked are drawn.
y-m-05-07.s.s3.hint.1: A case where a side would be a line that is not drawn should not be counted as a triangle.
y-m-05-07.s.s3.placeholder: Example: There are ... triangles. The way I counted is ...
y-m-05-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check that all three sides are drawn when you picked three points?
y-m-05-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you mention the cases that cannot be a triangle because ㄴ and ㄹ are not joined?
y-m-05-07.s.s3.model.0: There are 2. They are ㄱㄴㄷ and ㄱㄷㄹ. Only places where a line is drawn can be used as a side, so without ㄴㄹ no other triangle can be made.
y-m-05-07.s.s3.model.1: The diagonal ㄱㄷ splits the square into two triangles, so there are 2. I picked 3 points and checked that all three sides are drawn.
y-m-05-07.s.s2.hint.0: Check one by one whether what was counted or chosen in each line really becomes a triangle in the picture.
y-m-05-07.s.s2.explain: It first goes wrong in line 3. ㄱ, ㅁ, and ㄷ are on one straight line (a diagonal), so they do not make a triangle. For the same reason ㄴ, ㅁ, and ㄹ must also be left out, so there are 8 triangles in all. The 9 in line 4 is wrong because it is a conclusion that carries on the mistake in line 3.

y-m-05-08.title: Who is taller, 98cm or 1m 5cm?
y-m-05-08.topic: Lengths written with both m and cm
y-m-05-08.goal: Realize that comparing lengths with different units by looking only at the numbers gives a wrong answer. Compare by changing to the same unit, and explain it to a younger sibling in easy words.
y-m-05-08.material: 1m is 100cm. If a height is written as 1m 5cm, it is the length of 1m and 5cm together. Sua's height is 1m 5cm, and Jiho's height is 98cm. To find out who is taller, Ido solved it as below.
y-m-05-08.thinking.0: Finding the wrong line in a solution
y-m-05-08.thinking.1: Changing between m and cm to make lengths that fit a condition
y-m-05-08.thinking.2: Explaining again to suit the listener
y-m-05-08.prereq.1: Reading and writing lengths using cm and m together
y-m-05-08.s.s1.hint.1: Put 1m 5cm and 98cm in the same unit and compare them with Ido's conclusion.
y-m-05-08.s.s1.line.0: Sua's height is 1m 5cm, and Jiho's height is 98cm.
y-m-05-08.s.s1.line.2: 98 is bigger than 1 or 5, so Jiho's height is bigger.
y-m-05-08.s.s1.line.3: So Jiho is taller than Sua.
y-m-05-08.s.s2.prompt: Write three different heights, as 'm m cm', that are taller than Sua's height (1m 5cm) and shorter than 1m 20cm. (m is a natural number that is 0 or more, and cm is a natural number from 0 to 99.)
y-m-05-08.s.s2.hint.0: Put 1m 5cm and 1m 20cm side by side in the same unit, and first decide a height that falls between them.
y-m-05-08.s.s2.hint.1: Split the height you chose back into 'm and cm' and check that the cm part does not go over 99.
y-m-05-08.s.s2.var.m: The m part of the height
y-m-05-08.s.s2.var.c: The cm part of the height
y-m-05-08.s.s2.ok.c1: m and cm are natural numbers in the right ranges.
y-m-05-08.s.s2.fail.c1: The cm part must be from 0 to 99. When it reaches 100cm, write it as 1m instead.
y-m-05-08.s.s2.fail.c2: It is not taller than Sua's height. Change both heights to the same unit and compare them.
y-m-05-08.s.s2.fail.c3: It is not shorter than 1m 20cm. Change both heights to the same unit and compare them.
y-m-05-08.s.s2.explain: 1m 5cm is 105cm and 1m 20cm is 120cm. The heights in between are 106cm to 119cm, so anything from 1m 6cm to 1m 19cm works. When the cm part reaches 100 or more, you must carry it up to m when you write it.
y-m-05-08.s.s3.prompt: A first-grade sibling said, "98 is bigger than 1 or 5, so Jiho is taller." Tell your sibling in easy words why you must not compare like that, so that they can understand.
y-m-05-08.s.s3.hint.0: Think of something to say that first asks whether the numbers your sibling compared are written in the same unit.
y-m-05-08.s.s3.hint.1: Explain in words your sibling can understand how many cm long 1m 5cm is.
y-m-05-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say in easy words that m and cm are different units?
y-m-05-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you compare the value of 1m 5cm changed to cm with 98cm?
y-m-05-08.s.s3.model.0: 1m is 100cm. So 1m 5cm is 105cm. If you put it in the same unit as 98cm, 105 is bigger. So Sua is taller.
y-m-05-08.s.s3.model.1: m and cm are different units, so you must not compare just the numbers. 1m is 100cm, so Sua is 105cm and Jiho is 98cm.
y-m-05-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose the line in Ido's solution where the heights are first compared wrongly. (Lines are numbered from 1.)
y-m-05-08.s.s1.hint.0: In the lines where the words comparing heights appear, check whether the units attached after the compared numbers are the same.
y-m-05-08.s.s1.line.1: 1m 5cm is the length of 1m and 5cm added together, and Jiho's 98cm is a length of 98cm.
y-m-05-08.s.s1.explain: It first compares wrongly in line 3. 1 is m, 5 is cm, and 98 is cm, so numbers with different units cannot be compared as they are. 1m 5cm is 105cm, which is longer than 98cm. The conclusion in line 4 comes from the wrong comparison in line 3, so it is a mistake that follows after it.
